newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: US fears stalemate at Geneva arms talks.
newsitem.headline: US fears stalemate at Geneva arms talks.

text.p: The United States fears a stalemate in the Conference on Disarmament, where non-aligned and Western countries remain at odds over the negotiating agenda for 1997, U.S. ambassador Stephen Ledogar said on Thursday.
In speeches to the 61-member body, France and Germany called for negotiations to halt production of fissile material used for nuclear weapons and a global ban on anti-personnel landmines.
But Egypt criticised the reluctance of the declared nuclear powers (Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States) to enter into negotiations on complete nuclear disarmament.
The talks, sponsored by the United Nations, opened an eight- week session on Tuesday yet lack a formal negotiating agenda due to disagreement over how far to go in the nuclear weapons field.

Ledogar accused some states of pushing the five declared nuclear powers to launch negotiations on total disarmament while allegedly producing fissile material (plutonium and highly-enriched uranium) for their own nuclear weapons.
"It is going to be slow. The fear is we will have a stalemate," Ledogar told Reuters after Thursday's session.
"I am not predicting one, but we are trying to figure out ways to avoid it.

"Some countries want the five nuclear powers to talk about nuclear disarmament in a time-bound period, while they themselves continue to produce fissile material for weapons," the U.S. disarmament envoy added. "It is a bizarre idea."
Western countries favour pushing ahead with negotiations to halt production of fissile material, known as "cut-off" talks. They are also ready to negotiate a global landmines ban.
But India and Pakistan are leading a non-aligned campaign to force the major powers to set up a committee to negotiate total nuclear disarmament within a set timetable, diplomats say.
Only then would the non-aligned countries be prepared to push ahead on cut-off as part of a nuclear disarmament package, they add.
The Conference agreed in March 1995 to negotiate a treaty to halt production of fissile material, but the talks never got off the ground as a nuclear test ban treaty took precedence.
France's ambassador Joelle Bourgois said: "If negotiations can start on cut-off, France will do all in its power to favour its quick launching and prompt conclusion."
Germany's senior envoy Wolfgang Hoffmann also called for substantial negotiations on fissile material, saying it would cap the amount available for nuclear weapons.

"The German government attaches high priority to the immediate commencement of negotiations on such a convention as a further important contribution towards non-proliferation and nuclear disarmament," he said.

In a message to the Geneva forum on Tuesday, U.S. President Bill Clinton said: "Effectively cutting off the spigot for more nuclear weapons is a necessary step toward, and would greatly contribute to, the ultimate goal of nuclear disarmament."

But Egypt's ambassador Mounir Zahran said on Thursday: "Notwithstanding the will of the overwhelming majority of the members of the international community, nuclear disarmament continues to progress at a very slow pace without a legally binding commitment to a time-bound framework for the achievement of complete nuclear disarmament."
"Such a stance would seem to indicate that countries possessing nuclear weapons are still considering that these weapons have a role to play in international relations."
